summary: An informational memo that describes in detail the TIFF-F profile of the Tag Image File Format, used for storing facsimile images. It documents the profile that fax software already used.

plainLanguage.summary: A fax is just a black and white picture of a page. This memo explains exactly how to save that picture in a standard file.

questions: what is the faxbw application parameter
how are fax pages stored in a tiff file
what is the tiff-f minimum subset
subtitle: The written-down recipe for storing black-and-white fax pages in a TIFF file.

tldr.problem: TIFF-F, the way fax software stored fax pages in TIFF files, had been folklore with no standard reference definition.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC takes Baseline TIFF as a starting point and lists which fields and values a fax file uses, how pages are laid out, and a minimum subset that old readers can handle.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard, and it also defines the faxbw application parameter for the image/tiff media type.

today: RFC 2306 is an Informational memo from March 1998; it is not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TIFF-F Needed Writing Down
sections.content:
TIFF-F is the F profile of the Tag Image File Format (TIFF) for facsimile. The RFC says it had been in common use for many years but never documented as a standard. An informal document was first created by a small group of fax experts led by Joe Campbell, and TIFF 6.0 notes that TIFF-F exists without defining it.

Historically the format was called TIFF Class F. TIFF 6.0 dropped the Class idea in favor of Baseline TIFF, so this RFC defines TIFF-F as Baseline TIFF plus the differences that apply to fax. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of fax programs already saved pages in the same kind of file, but nobody had written down the rules. This memo finally writes them down.

sections.title: How a TIFF-F File Is Organized
sections.content:
A TIFF file starts with an 8-byte header that gives the byte order, a magic number and an offset to the first Image File Directory (IFD). An IFD is a list of tagged fields, sorted by tag value, that describes an image and points at its data.

In TIFF-F each fax page has its own IFD, and the IFDs form a linked list in which the last pointer is 0. Writers SHOULD put IFDs in page order, number pages from 0, and keep each page's image data in a single strip. Each IFD SHOULD come before the image it describes. Readers SHOULD still accept the more flexible layouts allowed by TIFF itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A fax file is like a binder. Each page has a cover sheet that says how big it is and where the picture is, and the sheets are kept in order.

sections.title: Required Fields and Values
sections.content:
TIFF-F uses all the Baseline TIFF fields for bi-level images but narrows the allowed values. Compression is 3 (T.4 Modified Huffman or Modified READ) or 4 (T.6 Modified Modified READ); uncompressed data is not allowed. PhotometricInterpretation is 0 (normal) or 1 (inverted). BitsPerSample and SamplesPerPixel are 1.

ImageWidth depends on resolution: 1728, 2048 or 2432 for the 200 and 204 dpi family, 2592, 3072 or 3648 for 300x300, and 3456, 4096 or 4864 for 400 and 408. Each file must also carry T4Options (for compression 3) or T6Options (for compression 4). FillOrder may be 1 or 2, and readers must handle both, though most fax products store data least significant bit first, as it appears on the phone line.

NewSubFileType has bit 1 set to mark a single page of a multi-page document, and PageNumber holds the page number and the total, so a single-page document is 0000/0001 in hex.
sections.plainLanguage: The cover sheet has a fixed list of boxes to fill in, like paper size and how the picture was squashed. Only certain answers are allowed.

sections.title: Compression, Page Quality and Optional Fields
sections.content:
Three compression methods are allowed. Modified Huffman (one-dimensional) is the most common and uses Compression 3 with bit 0 of T4Options equal to 0. Modified READ (two-dimensional) sets that bit to 1. MMR, also called Group 4, uses Compression 4, and each MMR strip MUST end with an end-of-facsimile-block (EOFB) code.

Writers SHOULD NOT put the Return To Control sequence (six consecutive EOLs) in T.4 data, but readers MUST cope without it and SHOULD cope with it. EOLs may be byte-aligned or not, controlled by bit 2 of T4Options.

Three optional fields describe how clean a received page was: BadFaxLines, CleanFaxData and ConsecutiveBadFaxLines. They SHOULD NOT be written for data that is error corrected or error free. Recommended informational fields include DateTime, DocumentName, ImageDescription, Orientation and Software.
sections.plainLanguage: Fax pages are squashed to save space, and there are three allowed ways to squash them. Optional notes can say how many lines got garbled on the phone line.

sections.title: The Minimum Subset, Readers and Writers
sections.content:
The minimum subset is the small set of values that should interwork with virtually all historic TIFF-F readers: Compression 3, FillOrder 2, ImageWidth 1728, XResolution 204 and YResolution 196 or 98, with RowsPerStrip equal to ImageLength. Minimum subset files MUST use the layout where each IFD, its long values and its image data come before the next page's IFD, and the header byte order SHOULD be II (little-endian).

A TIFF-F reader accepts either byte order (II or MM) and the full table of values. Writers SHOULD produce files a reader can read and include all the listed fields to avoid depending on defaults. For many Internet applications only the reader needs to be implemented. Streaming use of TIFF-F is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a safe, plain recipe that even the oldest fax programs can read. Newer programs may use fancier options, but should know the plain one.

sections.title: MIME Type and Security
sections.content:
TIFF-F content travels in the image/tiff media type. This RFC defines the optional application parameter value faxbw for black and white fax, for example Content-type: image/tiff; application=faxbw. It lets a recipient pick a suitable renderer before processing the image.

The RFC expects TIFF-F to be a component of Internet Fax, and mentions its use as a secondary component of a VPIM message. On security, it says the new fields are purely descriptive, so it creates no new risks beyond those already identified for the image/tiff registration, and it does not prevent use of any Internet security protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A label on the envelope says it is a black and white fax picture, so the receiver knows which program should open it.
